prompt.context: Your client is the State Department of Education and it is looking to improve the education outcomes of the general population. The department believes that investment in Pre-Kindergarten education (ages 3-4) is key and wants to increase the capacity of its state accredited Pre-K programs. The client is thinking about running a campaign to raise taxes to fund this initiative.
prompt.question: The client has come to us with three questions: (1) How many additional spots for children need to be funded for the Pre-K programs? (2) How much will the campaign cost? (3) How should they approach the tax increase campaign?

clarifying_info.q: What does 'improve education outcomes' mean specifically?
clarifying_info.a: Education outcome means college admittance and completion rates.

clarifying_info.q: Can the state rely on private Pre-K programs to help meet the goal?
clarifying_info.a: Private Pre-K programs are highly fragmented and range widely in quality. The State Department of Education only wants to rely on state-funded programs in which they can guarantee quality (education level of teacher, full-day program with adequate teaching materials/supplies, etc.).

clarifying_info.q: Is this a new program or an expansion of an existing one?
clarifying_info.a: The State Department of Education has already launched a similar initiative and provided some funding. Now they want to expand the program.

clarifying_info.q: Will the program generate any revenue?
clarifying_info.a: No revenues — the program will be free. The state wants to limit capacity to only children from low-income families.

clarifying_info.q: What is the cost per spot?
clarifying_info.a: Cost per spot is $10,000 a year to the state.

clarifying_info.q: Who is eligible for these Pre-K spots?
clarifying_info.a: The program is for children from low-income families only — those who could not afford private programs.

clarifying_info.q: How is the population distributed by age?
clarifying_info.a: Population is experiencing steady growth. Assume equal distribution of children in each age among all kids ages 3–18.

framework: 1. Financial Considerations: (a) Total addressable market vs. current capacity, (b) Cost breakdown of adding new schools, (c) Taxpayer base and how to increase taxes

2. Strategic Considerations: (a) Other states that have launched Pre-K programs and their approach, (b) Role of private Pre-K programs in serving the state's goal, (c) Other pressing issues facing the city/school district — who else is competing for the same resources?
3. Operational Considerations: (a) Long-term impact of the funding initiative (to get taxpayers on board), (b) What is being taxed (real estate, sales, soda) and who is most directly affected?
Note: Candidate should recognize there is no revenue associated with the Pre-K program — it is a tradeoff between improving education outcomes and cost to the state.

questions.prompt: Brainstorm: What are some benefits to improving early education?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify both short-term and long-term benefits. Short-term: social and emotional development, learning colors, letters, etc. Long-term: higher high school graduation rates, better standardized test scores, reading/writing at grade level, college attendance and completion rates.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, how many additional spots need to be funded to reach the State Department of Education's goal of providing Pre-K education to all children of low-income families?
questions.guidance: Candidate must calculate Pre-K population per region (K-12 pop / 16 age years * 2 Pre-K years = Pre-K pop), then apply the low-income percentage to find total spots needed, then subtract current spots available. Key insight: some regions are overfunded (negative gap), so the net additional spots needed is far less than 400 — the state could reallocate rather than build new capacity. Candidate should flag over-funded regions (2, 4, 5) and ask why.

math.setup: Pre-K population = K-12 population / 16 * 2 (ages 3 and 4 out of ages 3-18 = 2 years out of 16). Total spots needed = Pre-K population * % low-income. Additional spots needed = Total spots needed - Current spots available.
math.answer: In total the state is over-capacity by ~4,752 spots. Only Regions 1 (+38) and 3 (+353) are underfunded. The state does not need to raise taxes to add spots — it should reallocate existing capacity from over-funded regions.

questions.prompt: Follow-up: Why do you think some of the regions are overfunded?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates will brainstorm structural reasons: demographic shifts (population moved out of Regions 2, 4, 5), historical over-investment, political reasons, or that the program was designed before current demographic data was available. Could also indicate that the regions have a mix of income levels that changed over time.

brainstorming.prompt: What are some benefits to improving early (Pre-K) education?

categories.name: Short-term developmental outcomes
ideas: Improved ability to sit still and focus

categories.name: Long-term academic outcomes
ideas: Reading and writing at grade level

categories.name: Societal and economic benefits
ideas: Higher future tax revenue from better-educated workforce
Attracting and retaining residents in the state

recommendation: Do NOT recommend launching a tax increase campaign or expanding the program at this time.
The data shows the state is actually over-capacity by ~4,752 spots in aggregate; Regions 2, 4, and 5 are significantly overfunded.
The state should first reallocate existing resources from over-funded regions to under-served Regions 1 and 3 before seeking new funding.
The effectiveness of the current program is also unproven — last year's graduates did not show strong results on social and aptitude-for-learning skills tests.
risks: The state continues to fall behind in education standards, making it difficult to attract and retain residents.
Poor early education outcomes may compound over time if the program flaws are not addressed.
The inconclusive test results may be a flaw in the test itself rather than the program — this needs to be validated before drawing conclusions.
next_steps: Reallocate spots from over-funded regions (2, 4, 5) to under-funded regions (1, 3).
Investigate why certain regions are overfunded — demographic data, enrollment trends, historical allocation decisions.
Improve the effectiveness of the existing Pre-K program by changing the curriculum or piloting different teaching approaches.
Develop better or alternative metrics to measure program performance beyond the current aptitude test.
Only consider a tax increase campaign after demonstrating replicable, positive program outcomes.
